name: Meats
description: Plain cooked meat is the closest thing to a cat's natural diet and the easiest treat to get right.
whyGood: Cats are obligate carnivores. Chicken, turkey and rabbit give them complete animal protein and the amino acids, like taurine, they cannot make themselves.
howToServe: Cooked plain, with no salt, oil, onion or garlic. Remove all bones and skin, cut into small pieces, and keep it to a small portion alongside their usual food.
avoid: Raw meat (risk of salmonella and toxoplasma), cooked bones (they splinter), processed meats such as ham, bacon or sausage, and anything seasoned.
tip: Treats of any kind should stay under about 10% of your cat's daily calories. Their complete food still does the real work.

name: Fish
description: Salmon and mackerel provide omega-3s that are good for the skin and coat.
whyGood: A source of omega-3 fatty acids and lean protein, good for the skin and the coat.
howToServe: Cooked, boneless, in small amounts and only occasionally.
avoid: Raw fish (risk of parasites), fish in excess (it can unbalance vitamin B1 intake), and tuna in large quantities.
tip: Once or twice a week at most, and never as the only source of protein.

name: Eggs
description: A well-cooked egg is a cheap, highly digestible protein treat that most cats enjoy.
whyGood: Eggs carry every essential amino acid in a form cats digest easily, plus vitamin A, B vitamins and selenium for the skin and coat.
howToServe: Fully cooked and plain — boiled or scrambled with no butter, oil, salt or milk. A teaspoon or two is a whole portion for an average cat.
avoid: Raw egg white, which contains avidin and blocks biotin absorption, and raw egg in general because of salmonella. Never add seasoning.
tip: Cook it through: raw egg is the one form that does more harm than good.

name: Fruits & vegetables
description: A few are safe in small amounts, but cats gain little from plants and some are outright toxic.
whyGood: Cooked pumpkin, carrot, green beans and courgette add fibre and water, which can help with hairballs and mild constipation. Small pieces of melon or blueberry are safe as an occasional novelty.
howToServe: Washed, peeled where relevant, cooked plain and cut small. Offer a teaspoon at a time and stop if it upsets their stomach.
avoid: Onion, garlic, leek, shallot and chives in every form, including powders — they damage red blood cells. Also grapes and raisins (kidney failure), avocado, unripe tomato, and raw potato.
tip: Cats have no dietary need for plants. Treat these as an occasional extra, never as a way to bulk out a meal.

name: Dairy
description: Most adult cats are lactose intolerant, so the saucer of milk is a myth worth retiring.
whyGood: A pea-sized piece of hard cheese is a useful high-value treat for giving medication or for training, and plain yoghurt is tolerated by some cats.
howToServe: Only in tiny amounts, and only if your cat has shown no reaction before. Hard, aged cheeses and plain unsweetened yoghurt are the lowest in lactose.
avoid: Cow's milk and cream, which commonly cause diarrhoea and bloating in adult cats. Also flavoured or sweetened yoghurt, and anything containing the sweetener xylitol.
tip: Kittens lose the enzyme that digests milk as they wean. An adult cat asking for milk still cannot handle it — offer water instead.

name: Dangerous foods
description: Some everyday foods are toxic to cats even in small amounts. These should never be offered or left within reach.
avoid: Chocolate and caffeine (theobromine and caffeine cause tremors and heart problems), onion, garlic, leek and chives, grapes and raisins, alcohol, raw yeast dough, macadamia nuts, and the sweetener xylitol found in sugar-free gum and sweets.
tip: If you think your cat has eaten any of these, call your vet or an animal poison line straight away — do not wait for symptoms.
